questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.

__This was not only exciting but rewarding__ because I was able to experience adventure for the first time in my life.

options.text: This was not only exciting but also rewarding
This was not only excited but also rewarding
This was not only exciting but also rewarded

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. This was not only exciting but also rewarding.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__ **

 
• The original sentence uses the correlative conjunction "not only... but...". 
 
• The grammatically complete and standard form of this correlative conjunction is "not only... but also...". The inclusion of "also" completes the idiomatic pair and emphasizes the second element. 
 
• Correlative conjunctions require parallelism. This means the grammatical structure of the phrase following "not only" must match the structure of the phrase following "but also". 
 
• In the given sentence, "exciting" and "rewarding" are both present participles functioning as adjectives, thus maintaining parallelism. The issue is the missing "also".

Let's analyze the options:

 
• 1) This was not only exciting but also rewarding: This option correctly completes the correlative conjunction with "also" and maintains the parallelism (adjective 'exciting' and adjective 'rewarding'). This is the most appropriate substitution.
 
• 2) This was not only excited but also rewarding: "Excited" is a past participle primarily describing a state of feeling (e.g., "I was excited"). Here, we need an adjective describing the nature of the experience itself, which "exciting" (causing excitement) correctly does. Thus, this option introduces a grammatical error.
 
• 3) No substitution: While understandable, the phrase "not only... but..." is less formal and complete than "not only... but also...", which is preferred in standard English.
 
• 4) This was not only exciting but also rewarded: "Rewarded" is a past participle that means 'given a reward'. "Rewarding" (something that provides satisfaction or benefit) is the correct adjective to maintain parallelism with "exciting". Thus, this option changes the meaning and introduces an error in parallelism.

Correct sentence: *This was not only exciting but also rewarding because I was able to experience adventure for the first time in my life*.

questions.question: Select the option that has used the correct tense.

options.text: He realised he had forgotten his keys after he had leave the house.
He realised he had forgotten his keys after he had left the house.
He realised he had forgotten his keys after he has leave the house.
He realised he had forgotten his keys after he was left the house.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. He realised he had forgotten his keys after he had left the house .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence involves the use of the **past perfect tense** to indicate the sequence of events in the past.
 
• In the sentence, the action of "leaving the house" occurred **before** the action of "realising" and "forgetting the keys."
 
• The correct construction uses the **past perfect tense** for the earlier action (had left the house) and the **simple past tense** for the later action (realised).

Correct sentence: *He realised he had forgotten his keys after he had left the house*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Option 1:** "had leave" is grammatically incorrect. The correct past participle of "leave" is "left."
 
• **Option 3:** "has leave" is incorrect because "has" is present perfect and does not fit the context of the past sequence of events.
 
• **Option 4:** "was left" suggests a passive voice, which changes the meaning of the sentence and is incorrect in this context.
 
 
 
• **Usage of past perfect:**
 
 
• Past perfect is used to indicate the earlier of two past actions in a sentence.
 
• Example: By the time I arrived, they **had left**.

questions.question:
Select the appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the following sentence to make it grammatically correct.

She is the most active and __the more__ energetic social worker in our team.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. the most .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence mentions two qualities about the subject: being active and energetic. When comparing the subject to others, the use of superlative adjectives is appropriate.
 
• The word **"more"** is used for comparative degree, but since the sentence already uses **"most active"** (superlative degree), the adjective **"energetic"** should also follow the superlative form.
 
• The correct substitution for **"more energetic"** is **"the most energetic"**.

Correct sentence: *She is the most active and the most energetic social worker in our team*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Superlative Degree:**
 
 
• **Structure:** The + adjective in superlative form.
 
• **Example:** She is the tallest girl in the class.
 
• **Usage:** Used to compare one entity to all others in a group.
 
 
 
• **Comparative Degree:**
 
 
• **Structure:** More + adjective (or adjective + -er).
 
• **Example:** She is more intelligent than her peers.
 
• **Usage:** Used to compare two entities.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.

We rely on Hiren because he is __most intelligent__ than many other boys in our school quiz team.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '4' i.e. more intelligent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence contains the phrase **"most intelligent"**, which is incorrect for comparison between two groups or individuals.
 
• When comparing one person with others in a group, the correct comparative form of the adjective must be used. In this case, **"more intelligent"** is appropriate.
 
• The sentence should use the comparative form because Hiren's intelligence is being compared to that of other boys in the quiz team.

Correct sentence: *We rely on Hiren because he is **more intelligent** than many other boys in our school quiz team.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Adjective Degrees of Comparison:**

 
 
• **Positive:** Describes one person or thing without comparison (e.g., intelligent).
 
• **Comparative:** Used for comparing two people or things (e.g., more intelligent).
 
• **Superlative:** Used for comparing one person or thing to a group (e.g., most intelligent).
 
 
 
• In this case, the comparative form **"more intelligent"** is correct because it compares Hiren's intelligence to other boys in the team.
